catalog_quote: 3.3 Tones Ywom Project (2011) claims that Ywom has three level tones, but does not present an example of three-way contrast. Although many other languages in Chadic A3 do appear to have three tones, such as Mwaghavul, Ywom almost certainly has two tones and occasional mid-tones are almost certainly phonetic. Minimal pairs are as follows; wóŋ song wòŋ to wash mí one mì relation túŋ sit down tùŋ ant-hill túk soup tùk to kill There are surface glide tones, rising and falling, but there are almost certainly the output from sequences of level tones. The most striking feature of Ywom is the presence of tones on deleted vowels. Many of the modified initial consonants in Ywom are in fact sequences of two consonants with a tone-bearing epenthetic vowel between them. For example, two common numerals, written flu and tra in the orthography are actually; Two fˊlù Ten tˋrá ... Ywom also has initial tone-bearing homorganic nasals. As with Mwaghavul, these are only sometimes sounded, for reasons which are still unclear.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ywom is described as a two-tone (H/L) language; surface mid tones are treated as phonetic and rising/falling glides as sequences of level tones; tones are retained on deleted vowels (e.g. 'two' fˊlù, 'ten' tˋrá). The source says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be extracted; only the tonal characterisation is on record.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; the tonal analysis is explicitly provisional ('almost certainly'), based on one recording (Ruth Pam, Jos, April 2012), and disputes the three-level-tone claim of Ywom Project (2011).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms from a wordlist elicitation; no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench's 'Ywom' = Yiwom yiwo1237 (also Gerka, Gerkawa, Gerkanci, Yioum); data from a single speaker (Ruth Pam) recorded in Jos, April 2012, representing the Hɨl Ywom community in Mikang LGA; no dialect division is described.

sources.note: Section 3 'Ywom phonology' (3.1 consonants, 3.2 vowels, 3.3 tones, pp. 1-5) never mentions stress or accent; 3.3 (p. 5) states Ywom 'almost certainly has two tones', mid tones phonetic, glide tones from level-tone sequences, tones survive on deleted vowels; minimal pairs given. Recovered via the Internet Archive (rogerblench.info is now a squatted domain).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2013. However did Ywom become so strange? Slides presented at BICCL 7, Hamburg, 12-14 September 2013, Asien-Afrika-Institut, Hamburg University. 34 slides.
